objectives: Explain how heat, cold, water removal and acids preserve food

blocks.title: Principles
blocks.md: Preservation prevents or slows spoilage by controlling **temperature** (heat destroys microorganisms; cold slows growth), **water** (drying, salting, sugaring), **acidity** (pickling, fermentation), **oxygen** (vacuum, sealing) and **time**. Methods are often combined, e.g. smoking = drying + chemicals from smoke + often salting.

blocks.title: Heat treatments
blocks.md: **Pasteurisation** (e.g. about 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds for milk, or 63 degrees for 30 minutes) kills disease-causing bacteria but not all microorganisms, so milk still needs refrigeration. **Sterilisation / canning** (about 121 degrees for low-acid foods) destroys nearly all microorganisms and spores; the sealed can is stable without refrigeration. Values are textbook figures flagged for review.

blocks.caption: A flow of four steps for processing cassava into garri.
blocks.alt: Flow of garri production: peel and wash, grate and ferment then press, sieve and roast, cool and store dry.

blocks.title: Local processing
blocks.md: **Drying** of fish, crayfish, maize and beans; **smoking** of fish and meat; **milling** of maize and rice; **fermentation** of cassava and cereal products, and traditional drinks; **frying and roasting** of snacks. **Cassava** (especially bitter varieties) contains natural cyanogenic compounds, which are reduced by peeling, grating, soaking, fermenting, pressing, drying and cooking; incomplete processing is a health risk.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Pasteurised does not mean sterile.
- Dried food rehydrates and spoils if stored in damp places.
- Smoked foods should be eaten in moderation (smoke can contain harmful compounds).
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Why pasteurise?
blocks.statement: Why is pasteurised milk still stored in a fridge?
steps: Pasteurisation kills disease-causing bacteria but not all microorganisms.
Cold storage slows the growth of the survivors.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Cassava safety
blocks.statement: Why must bitter cassava be processed properly?
steps: It contains compounds that can release cyanide.
Peeling, grating, fermenting, pressing, drying and cooking reduce them.

objectives: Explain how nutritional needs change with age and condition
Plan meals for infants, children, adolescents, pregnant and elderly people in outline
Use food groups and cost to plan
Adapt for special diets in general terms
reviewNotes: Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.
Infant feeding statements follow WHO general guidance and must be checked against national guidelines by a nutritionist or paediatric health worker.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Needs change
blocks.md: **Infants**: breast milk alone is recommended for about the first six months (WHO guidance), then **complementary foods** while breastfeeding continues. **Children**: frequent small meals, growth needs protein, energy, iron, calcium. **Adolescents**: rapid growth, higher needs for energy, iron (especially girls after periods start) and calcium. **Adults**: maintenance, according to activity. **Pregnancy and breastfeeding**: extra energy and nutrients (iron, folate, iodine, calcium) under health-worker guidance. **Older adults**: less energy, but similar protein, calcium, vitamin D and fluid needs.

blocks.title: Planning steps
blocks.md: 1. Identify the group and its needs. 2. Choose a staple, a protein food and vegetables or fruit for each meal. 3. Add healthy snacks (groundnuts, fruit). 4. Adapt texture (soft foods for infants and some older people). 5. Check hygiene, cost and cultural acceptability. 6. Review with a health worker if the person is ill or pregnant.

blocks.caption: A table of four groups and their important nutritional needs.
blocks.alt: Table: infants need breast milk and energy, adolescents iron and calcium, pregnant women iron and folate, older adults calcium and fluids.

blocks.title: Special diets (general)
blocks.md: Some people need special diets, such as low-salt or low-sugar diets for medical reasons, or exclude foods because of allergies or beliefs. These must be set with health professionals. Teachers and cooks should not recommend therapeutic diets for illnesses on their own.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Giving infants thin porridge with little energy or protein.
- Giving honey to infants under one year (not recommended by health authorities).
- Using very low-fat or strict diets for growing children without advice.
- Nutrition, health and food-safety statements are textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian, food scientist or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Infant
blocks.statement: A mother of a 7-month-old baby asks what to give. Give general advice.
steps: Continue breastfeeding and add soft, well-cooked foods in small amounts, such as enriched pap (with groundnut paste, fish or egg) and mashed fruit and vegetables.
Keep utensils clean, prepare fresh food, and see a clinic for individual advice.
blocks.answer: Continue breastfeeding; add enriched soft foods; clinic advice

blocks.title: Example 2 - Adolescent
blocks.statement: A 15-year-old girl feels tired and eats little meat or beans. Which nutrient might be low and what is the advice?
steps: Iron is commonly low in adolescent girls; fatigue has many causes.
Add iron-rich foods with vitamin C and visit a health worker for assessment.
